title: The New MacBook Pro's Touch Display Is Something Special
gist: WIRED rates Apple's 2026 OLED MacBook Pro 8/10, praising its tandem 'PROLED XDR' display (1,000 nits SDR, up to 2,000 nits HDR), removal of the notch and lighter weight, but calling the touchscreen half-baked. It reuses last year's M5 Pro/M5 Max chips, a first for Apple Silicon, and costs $400 more than the Mini-LED model on top of an earlier $500 price rise, with the reviewer citing a tightening memory shortage as reason prices won't fall.

themes.theme: Apple product strategy shift: OLED and touch on Mac

insights.claim: Apple now sells two versions of its flagship MacBook Pro: a Mini-LED model with the new M6 processor and an OLED touchscreen model, which the reviewer calls the biggest MacBook Pro change since 2021.
insights.speaker: Luke Larsen
insights.so_what: A tiered premium Mac lineup lets Apple push average selling prices higher via a display-led upsell.
insights.locator: With the arrival of the OLED

insights.claim: The reviewer judges Apple's Mac touchscreen a 'catch-up' feature that does not aim to replace keyboard and trackpad, citing clumsy touch on small macOS controls, no Apple Pencil support, no convertible hinge, and dependence on third-party developers to optimize apps for touch.
insights.speaker: Luke Larsen
insights.so_what: Touch is unlikely to be a major upgrade driver on its own, limiting its contribution to Mac unit growth.
insights.quote: This feels more like a “catch-up” feature we’ve long been without

insights.claim: Apple is marketing the touchscreen to creative professionals with features in Pixelmator Pro, ZBrush and Logic Pro, but the reviewer regards these as more gimmick than real benefit and says he will wait for Adobe to prove otherwise.
insights.speaker: Luke Larsen
insights.so_what: Adoption by major third-party software vendors like Adobe will determine whether touch becomes a meaningful Mac ecosystem feature.
insights.locator: Apple has been selling the OLED

insights.claim: The OLED MacBook Pro's tandem OLED panel, first used in the iPad Pro over two years ago, reaches 1,000 nits in SDR and was measured at 1,849 nits peak HDR (rated 2,000), making it the brightest laptop display the reviewer has tested, though only 12 percent brighter than the Mini-LED model.
insights.speaker: Luke Larsen
insights.so_what: Tandem OLED migrating from tablets to laptops supports demand for premium OLED panel suppliers.

insights.claim: OLED's thinner layers cut the 16-inch model's weight to 4 pounds, well over half a pound lighter than the non-OLED equivalent, and a hole-punch camera with Dynamic Island replaces the notch.
insights.speaker: Luke Larsen
insights.so_what: Tangible form-factor gains give Apple a hardware differentiation story despite flat chip performance.
insights.locator: Another discernible difference in the OLED

insights.claim: The reviewer hopes that as HDR-capable devices like the OLED MacBook Pro proliferate, more HDR video will be produced, even for the web.
insights.speaker: Luke Larsen
insights.so_what: Wider HDR hardware base could gradually shift content production standards.

insights.claim: The 2026 OLED MacBook Pro reuses the previous generation's M5 Pro and M5 Max chips, the first time since Apple Silicon's 2020 debut that a new Mac has not come with an updated chip, and benchmarks such as Cinebench 2026 show performance parity with last year's model.
insights.speaker: Luke Larsen
insights.so_what: Either Apple's silicon pace is slowing or it is betting on display features to drive refresh, a notable change in Mac upgrade dynamics.
insights.quote: Either Apple’s pace is slowing down, or the company thinks the OLED touchscreen will be a strong enough draw to convince buyers to refresh.

insights.claim: Rumors cited by the reviewer say Apple may skip the M6 Pro and M6 Max entirely and save higher-end configurations for the M7 generation, which would also be a first for Apple Silicon.
insights.speaker: Luke Larsen
insights.so_what: A skipped high-end generation could lengthen pro Mac replacement cycles.

insights.claim: The reviewer says the M5 Max still dominates in overall power even against new Nvidia RTX Spark laptops such as the Microsoft Surface Laptop Ultra.
insights.speaker: Luke Larsen
insights.so_what: Apple retains a performance lead over Nvidia-powered Windows laptops, giving it room to slow its chip cadence.

insights.claim: Owners of M5 Pro or M5 Max MacBook Pros will find the OLED version hard to justify, so the reviewer expects many buyers to wait until next year for a performance upgrade.
insights.speaker: Luke Larsen
insights.so_what: Limited upgrade incentive for recent buyers may dampen near-term high-end Mac sell-through.

themes.theme: Rising prices and the memory shortage

insights.claim: The OLED MacBook Pro costs $400 more than the Mini-LED model, on top of an earlier-this-year price increase that added $500 to the M5 Max MacBook Pro; the 14-inch starts at $2,899, the 16-inch at $3,399, and the tested M5 Max 128 GB/2 TB configuration costs $7,399.
insights.speaker: Luke Larsen
insights.so_what: Apple is pushing premium pricing sharply higher, testing demand elasticity at the top of the laptop market.

insights.claim: The reviewer sees little hope that MacBook Pro prices will come down soon because the memory shortage continues to tighten.
insights.speaker: Luke Larsen
insights.so_what: Memory scarcity is feeding through to premium PC pricing, a tailwind for memory makers and a margin or demand headwind for OEMs.
insights.quote: There’s little hope prices will come down anytime soon, as the memory shortage continues to tighten.
